opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it wasn't some grand, carefully planned decision. When I first went to talk with Professor Zhu, I was still an undergrad and didn't have a clear picture of what I wanted to do. I just knew I liked writing code and building things, and I was curious about AI because it felt like the most exciting thing happening at the time.

He laid out a few directions the lab was working on, and reinforcement learning stood out to me. It felt closer to what I imagined "intelligence" to be. With supervised learning you're fitting a dataset someone already labeled. With RL you have an agent interacting with an environment, trying things, failing, and gradually figuring out how to get better. That loop of trial and error felt very natural, almost like how people learn.

Around that time there were also a lot of striking results, like agents playing Atari games and AlphaGo. Seeing a system learn to do something impressive from just a reward signal was really inspiring.

There was also a practical side. RL had a lot of engineering pain back then. Experiments were slow, codebases were messy, and results were hard to reproduce. As someone who enjoyed engineering, I saw that less as a downside and more as a place where I could contribute. That later turned into working on Tianshou, building a cleaner and faster RL framework, which in some ways shaped the rest of my path.

So it was a mix of curiosity about what intelligence looks like, excitement about the results, and a sense that my engineering skills could actually make a difference in that area.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it wasn't a very dramatic decision. When I was an undergrad at Tsinghua, I joined Professor Zhu's lab, and at that time the lab was working on a lot of different things: probabilistic models, generative models, Bayesian stuff, and also some reinforcement learning. When we sat down to talk about what I should work on, he laid out a few directions and asked what I was interested in.

What drew me to RL was that it felt like the part of machine learning that was closest to actually doing something. With supervised learning, you have a dataset, you fit a model, you report a number. With RL, you have an agent interacting with an environment, making decisions, getting feedback, and you can literally watch it get better or watch it fail in really strange ways. That loop was very appealing to me. I also had a background in programming competitions, so I liked systems, I liked building things, and RL at that time was a field where the infrastructure was honestly a mess. Everyone was writing their own training loops, their own replay buffers, and nothing was reproducible. I saw that as an opportunity rather than a problem.

Professor Zhu was very supportive of that. He didn't push me toward a specific paper or a specific benchmark. He basically said, if you think the tooling is a bottleneck, go fix the tooling, and the research will follow. That's eventually how Tianshou came about, the RL library I started building in the lab. So I would say the choice was partly about intellectual interest, and partly about matching what I was good at with where the field actually needed help.

r001.rationale: The response says Weng was offered several research directions and chose RL for its interactive feedback loop and tooling needs. It does not say Weng could not identify which direction was GANs.

When discussing research directions with Professor Jun Zhu, I found that way of thinking particularly interesting. It connects learning with decision-making, and that was the kind of problem I wanted to explore.

sol-6.1.text: What attracted me to reinforcement learning was the idea of learning through interaction. Rather than just making predictions from a fixed dataset, an agent takes actions and learns from their consequences. When discussing research directions with Professor Jun Zhu, that connection between learning and decision-making was what I wanted to explore. It also seemed like an area with a lot of open questions, which made it exciting as a research direction.
